## Slide Accessibility Note
- **Title Background Image Alt-Text:** A side-by-side comparison of a raw Quarto document output and a polished, formatted report with a table of contents, numbered sections, and captioned figures.
- **Speaker Notes:** These slides guide students through progressively polishing a Quarto document from a functional draft to a reader-facing report suitable for a thesis chapter or technical memo.

## Learning Objectives

1. Set document-level YAML options that control structure and code visibility.
2. Add figure and table captions with cross-references (`@fig-`, `@tbl-`).
3. Embed live data summaries using inline R expressions.
4. Create a parameterized report that can be rerun for different subgroups.
5. Format tables with `knitr::kable()` or `gt()`.

::: {.notes}
**Speaker Notes:**
This is Week 14 — the capstone week for reproducible workflows. Students have been writing Quarto documents all semester, but mostly for their own use. Today the audience shifts: we are writing for a reader who does not see the code. Every decision — hiding code, numbering sections, captioning figures — serves that reader.
:::

## The Problem with Drafts

- Raw output: code visible, figures unnumbered, tables print as tibbles.
- A reader cannot find Figure 3 if there is no Figure 3.
- Hard-coded numbers break the moment data changes.

**Today's goal:** make the document do the bookkeeping so you don't have to.

## How To Use Today

- Start with a document that renders, then polish the reader experience.
- Let Quarto number and reference figures and tables for you.
- Use inline R for values that should stay in sync with the data.

<a class="script-download" href="../scripts/week_14_follow_along.R" download style="background-color: #d00000 !important; color: #fff !important;">Download the Week 14 follow-along script (.R)</a>

::: {.notes}
**Speaker Notes:**
Open a "before" document on the projector — one that renders but is clearly not ready for a reader. Ask students what they notice. Common answers: you can see all the R warnings, the figure is just floating there with no number, the table is just a tibble dump. Use this as the motivation for every YAML option we add today.
:::

## Document-Level YAML: The Foundation

```yaml
---
title: "Nebraska Deer Harvest Report"
author: "Chris Chizinski"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    number-sections: true
    fig-width: 7
    fig-height: 4.5
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---
```

::: {.notes}
**Speaker Notes:**
Walk through each option. toc: true adds the sidebar navigation — readers can jump to a section. number-sections: true auto-numbers headings. embed-resources: true is critical: without it, sharing the HTML file means sharing a folder of assets too. echo: false at the document level means no code chunks appear in the output unless a specific chunk overrides with echo: true.
:::

## YAML Options at a Glance

| Option | Where | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `toc: true` | `format: html:` | Adds sidebar navigation |
| `number-sections: true` | `format: html:` | Auto-numbers headings |
| `fig-width` / `fig-height` | `format: html:` | Default figure dimensions |
| `embed-resources: true` | `format: html:` | Single portable file |
| `echo: false` | `execute:` | Hides code globally |
| `warning: false` | `execute:` | Suppresses warnings |
| `message: false` | `execute:` | Suppresses messages |
| `echo: true` | individual chunk `#|` | Override: show this chunk |

::: {.notes}
**Speaker Notes:**
Stress the two-level hierarchy: document-level execute: options set the default; individual chunk #| options override. This is how you hide data-loading code but show a key analysis chunk in a methods section.
:::

## Figure Captions and Cross-References

````markdown
```{{r}}
#| label: fig-harvest-trend
#| fig-cap: "Total Nebraska deer harvest by year across all seasons."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of deer harvest 2018–present with increasing trend."

deer |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(total = sum(harvest_count, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = total)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Total Harvest") +
  theme_minimal()
```
````

In prose: `"As shown in @fig-harvest-trend, harvest increased..."`

::: {.notes}
**Speaker Notes:**
The label must start with fig- for figure cross-references to work. The @fig-harvest-trend in prose renders as "Figure 1" — or whatever number the figure actually ends up being. The payoff: if you insert a new figure earlier in the document, all the downstream numbers update automatically. You never touch the prose. This is the core value of cross-referencing.
:::

## Why Cross-References Matter

- Hard-coded: *"As shown in Figure 3..."* → You add a figure → now it's Figure 4 → your prose is wrong.
- Cross-reference: *"As shown in @fig-harvest-trend..."* → Quarto handles the number → always correct.

Same logic applies to tables with `@tbl-`.

::: {.notes}
**Speaker Notes:**
Ask students how many times they have had to manually renumber figures in a Word document. The groan is universal. This is the exact problem cross-references solve. It is not a cosmetic feature — it is a correctness feature.
:::

## Formatted Tables: knitr::kable()

````markdown
```{{r}}
#| label: tbl-top-counties
#| tbl-cap: "Top 10 county-season combinations by total deer harvest."

deer |>
  group_by(county, season) |>
  summarize(total = sum(harvest_count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(total, n = 10) |>
  rename(County = county, Season = season, `Total Harvest` = total) |>
  knitr::kable()
```
````

In prose: `"County leaders are listed in @tbl-top-counties."`

::: {.notes}
**Speaker Notes:**
kable() is the simplest path to a formatted HTML table. It respects column names, so rename() before kable() is good practice. The label must start with tbl- for table cross-references. Show the rendered output side by side with the raw tibble print — the difference is obvious. If students want more control over column formatting, cell colors, or footnotes, point them toward gt() as an extension.
:::

## Inline R: Let the Data Write the Numbers

In your .qmd prose:

```markdown
The dataset covers `r n_distinct(deer$county)` counties and
`r n_distinct(deer$year)` harvest years, totalling
`r format(sum(deer$harvest_count, na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")`
individual deer harvested.
```

Renders as:

> The dataset covers 12 counties and 5 harvest years, totalling 48,302 individual deer harvested.

::: {.notes}
**Speaker Notes:**
The backtick-r syntax is how Quarto evaluates R code inline inside prose. Everything between the backticks runs as R. The result is inserted as plain text. Key point: when the data is updated next year, the numbers update automatically on the next render. No search-and-replace, no copy-paste errors. Ask students: "When would hard-coding the number be safer?" Answer: when the calculation is complex enough that an error would go unnoticed — then you want to compute it once, assign it to a named object, and reference the object inline.
:::

## Parameterized Reports

```yaml
params:
  county: "Lancaster"
  season: "archery"
```

```r
deer_sub <- deer |>
  filter(county == params$county,
         season == params$season)
```

Rerun for a different county at the terminal:

```bash
quarto render report.qmd -P county:Douglas -P season:firearm
```

::: {.notes}
**Speaker Notes:**
Ask: how many Nebraska counties are there? 93. If you needed a harvest report for every county, the copy-paste approach means 93 files with duplicated code, all of which drift out of sync. With params, you write one document and render it 93 times — or use a loop in a separate script to do it automatically. This is the gateway concept to literate programming at scale.
:::

## The Challenge [45 mins]

### The Report Polish Challenge

- Take your capstone analysis draft (or the deer harvest starter).
- Add: `toc`, `number-sections`, `echo: false`.
- Add one figure with `fig-cap` and reference it with `@fig-` in prose.
- Add one table using `knitr::kable()` with `tbl-cap` and `@tbl-` cross-reference.
- Add two inline R expressions reporting summary values.
- Add a `params:` block with one parameter.

**Base goal:** Make the draft readable and correctly referenced.

**Extension goal:** Parameterize the report so it can be rerun for different subgroups.

::: {.notes}
**Speaker Notes:**
Students who do not have a capstone draft ready should use the provided deer harvest starter .qmd. The challenge is designed to be completed in one session — the pieces are all covered in today's demo. Circulate and watch for the two most common errors: (1) labels that don't start with fig- or tbl-, and (2) inline expressions that fail because the object isn't defined earlier in the document.
:::

## Verification

- Render from a fresh R session (`Session > Restart R > Render`).
- All `@fig-` and `@tbl-` references resolve — no `?fig-` in the output.
- Inline R values match what you see in the console.
- The TOC has at least three entries.
- params block is tested with at least two different values.
- Can you explain why hard-coded figure numbers are a maintenance problem?

::: {.notes}
**Speaker Notes:**
The restart-and-render test is the gold standard for reproducibility. If the document only renders when your environment is already populated, it is not reproducible — it just looks like it is. Emphasize this before students submit their assignments: render from a clean session, not from the comfort of an open session where everything is already loaded.
:::
